title: Exploring Network Settings and Internet Connectivity
description: Discover your computer's network configuration using built-in tools and command prompt
objective: Students will explore their computer's network settings, identify IP addresses, test internet connectivity, and understand DNS resolution using Windows tools and Command Prompt

steps.title: Find Your Network Configuration
steps.instructions:
Let us find out how your computer is connected to the network.

**Step A: Using Windows Settings**
1. Click the **WiFi icon** in the taskbar (bottom-right corner)
2. Click **Properties** on your connected network
3. Scroll down and note these values:
   - **IPv4 address** (e.g., 192.168.1.105)
   - **DNS server** address
   - **Network type** (Private or Public)

**Step B: Using Command Prompt**
1. Press **Windows + R**, type `cmd`, press Enter
2. Type the following command and press Enter:
```
ipconfig
```
3. Find and write down:
   - **IPv4 Address:** _______________
   - **Subnet Mask:** _______________
   - **Default Gateway:** _______________

The Default Gateway is your **router's IP address** — the device that connects you to the internet.

**Question:** Is your IPv4 address a private IP or a public IP? How do you know?

*Hint:* Private IPs start with 192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x, or 172.16-31.x.x

steps.title: Test Your Internet Connection with Ping
steps.instructions:
The `ping` command tests whether your computer can reach another computer on the network or internet.

**In Command Prompt, run these tests one by one:**

**Test 1 — Ping your router:**
```
ping 192.168.1.1
```
(Replace with your Default Gateway address from Step 1)

If you get replies, your connection to the router is working.

**Test 2 — Ping Google's DNS server:**
```
ping 8.8.8.8
```
If you get replies, your internet connection is working.

**Test 3 — Ping a website by name:**
```
ping google.com
```
If this works, your DNS is working (converting names to IP addresses).

**Record your results:**
| Test | Target | Got Reply? | Average Time |
|------|--------|-----------|-------------|
| 1 | Router (gateway) | | |
| 2 | 8.8.8.8 | | |
| 3 | google.com | | |

**Troubleshooting logic:**
- Test 1 fails = WiFi/cable connection problem
- Test 2 fails but Test 1 works = Internet is down (ISP problem)
- Test 3 fails but Test 2 works = DNS problem

steps.title: Understand DNS in Action
steps.instructions:
DNS converts website names into IP addresses. Let us see it in action.

**In Command Prompt, run:**

```
nslookup google.com
```

This asks the DNS server: "What is the IP address of google.com?"

Note the **IP address** returned: _______________

Now try more websites:
```
nslookup irctc.co.in
nslookup digilocker.gov.in
nslookup techpath.biz
```

**Record the results:**
| Website | IP Address |
|---------|------------|
| google.com | |
| irctc.co.in | |
| digilocker.gov.in | |
| techpath.biz | |

Notice that some websites return multiple IP addresses. This is called **load balancing** — the website has many servers, and DNS distributes visitors among them.

**Try this experiment:**
1. Copy the IP address you got for google.com
2. Open Chrome and paste that IP address in the address bar
3. Does it open Google? This proves that DNS just converts the name to an IP — the IP is the real address!

**CCC Exam Connection:** DNS = Domain Name System = Phone book of the internet

steps.title: Trace the Route to a Website
steps.instructions:
When you visit a website, your data passes through many routers before reaching the destination. The `tracert` command shows every router (hop) along the way.

**In Command Prompt, run:**
```
tracert google.com
```

This may take 1-2 minutes. Each line shows one router your data passes through.

**Example output:**
```
 1    1 ms    1 ms    1 ms   192.168.1.1       <- Your router
 2    5 ms    4 ms    5 ms   10.0.0.1           <- ISP router
 3   12 ms   11 ms   12 ms  ...                 <- Internet backbone
 ...
12   35 ms   34 ms   36 ms  142.250.77.110     <- Google server
```

**Answer these questions:**
1. How many hops (routers) does it take to reach Google? ___
2. What is the first hop? (It should be your router) _______________
3. Which hop has the longest delay? _______________
4. Some hops may show `* * *` — this means that router blocks tracert requests. It is normal.

**Now trace another website:**
```
tracert irctc.co.in
```

Compare: Does irctc.co.in have more or fewer hops than Google? Why might this be?

**CCC Exam Connection:** Data travels through multiple routers, broken into packets, and reassembled at the destination.

steps.title: Identify Network Type and Connection Details
steps.instructions:
Let us identify what type of network you are using and gather all the important details.

**Step A: Identify your network type**

Open Command Prompt and run:
```
ipconfig /all
```

Find these details:
| Detail | Your Value | What It Means |
|--------|-----------|---------------|
| Connection Type (WiFi/Ethernet) | | WiFi = wireless, Ethernet = cable |
| DHCP Enabled | | Yes = IP assigned automatically |
| Physical Address (MAC) | | Unique hardware address of your network card |
| DNS Servers | | Server that converts domain names to IPs |
| IPv4 Address | | Your private IP on this network |
| Default Gateway | | Your router's IP address |

**Step B: What type of network is this?**
- Your classroom network is a: ___ (LAN / MAN / WAN)
- The internet you are accessing through it is a: ___ (LAN / MAN / WAN)
- Your WiFi connection uses which topology? ___ (Star / Bus / Ring)
  *Hint:* All devices connect to one central router

**Step C: Check your public IP**
Open Chrome and go to: https://www.whatismyip.com
- Public IP: _______________
- ISP Name: _______________

**Final Questions:**
1. Is your private IP the same as your public IP? Why?
2. What is the role of the router (Default Gateway) in your network?
3. What network device converts your computer's digital signals for internet use?

**Take screenshots of your ipconfig /all output and whatismyip.com result. Paste them in your lab report.**
